items.title: DJI Thermal Analyzer
items.text:
DJI Thermal Analyzer (the dji-thermal-ui command) analyzes, converts, mosaics and measures DJI thermal flights in the browser, on your own computer. It does the work with dji-thermal-cli, so neither ODM nor the DJI Thermal SDK is needed.

It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, for the one person using the computer: there are no logins or accounts.

  • Getting started: install it, run it, and find your way around its pages.
  • Quickstart: short tutorials, from a first flight to its report.
  • User guide: a page for each part of the app, named as the app names it.
  • Reference: the command, and where the data lives.

items.title: Finding your way
items.text: The app names its parts Project › Flight › Dataset: a project holds a site's flights, a flight holds the images of one flight of the drone, and a dataset is a flight's images converted to temperatures, with its mosaics.

items.title: The navigation pane
items.text:
A pane on the left of every page lists the projects, under each its flights, under each its datasets, then User Preferences, System Settings and Storage. The pages' own tabs and buttons go further: the viewer's tabs, Compare, the reports, the frames explorer.

  • A dataset opens its mosaics (else its frames, else its flight's Datasets tab), and is marked on any of its pages; a flight is marked on its Flight report.
  • Projects and flights fold. What the pane unfolds to show the page shown stays unfolded until folded.
  • The whole pane hides, by the header's menu button or the small tab on its edge. Over a narrow screen it opens on top of the page.
  • The box under Projects filters the projects by name, and stays as typed from page to page until it is emptied (Escape empties it).

items.title: The header
items.text: Beside the app's name, the header has the unit temperatures are shown in (°F, °C or K) and light or dark pages (or the computer's own), both also under User Preferences. Help opens this documentation in a new tab, at the page for the page you are on, and the version installed is beside it.

items.title: Searching
items.text: Every search in the app matches the same way, as you type: each word typed, in any order and any case ("roof north" finds "North roof"). User Preferences and System Settings have a filter at the top too, showing the sections whose title, labels, help or choices have the words typed ("dark" finds Theme).

items.title: First run
items.text:
dji-thermal-ui

This serves the app on http://127.0.0.1:8080 and opens it in the browser, on the projects page. Press Ctrl+C to stop it. A job still running when the server stops (an analysis, a conversion, a mosaic) is marked as interrupted the next time it starts. --port serves on another port, --no-browser leaves the browser closed, and --data-dir keeps the data in another folder: see The command.

The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, for the one person using the computer: there are no logins or accounts.

items.title: The first time
items.text: The data folder is made where your system keeps applications' data (see Where the data lives), with the database and a secret key in it, and a project called Default Project, which you can rename. Make a flight there with New Flight, or make a project of your own first: the Quickstart goes through it.

items.title: What needs the internet
items.text:
Everything works offline except:

  • The maps under the mosaics, loaded from Esri, OpenStreetMap or Mapbox as you look at them (see The maps under the mosaics). A map can show no basemap at all.
  • A project's location, searched for on OpenStreetMap's Nominatim: the text searched, or the point clicked, is sent to it by the app, at most once a second. The addresses are © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the ODbL.
  • WebODM, when you connect one (see WebODM), which may be on your own computer.

This documentation is served by the app itself, from the header's Help, so it works offline and matches the version installed.

items.title: Install
items.text: DJI Thermal Analyzer runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, and needs Python 3.12 or newer. It is not on PyPI yet.

items.title: From a built wheel
items.text:
The wheel holds everything, the pages and this documentation included, so installing it needs no Node.js:

uv tool install dji_thermal_ui-<version>-py3-none-any.whl

pipx install with the same file works too. Either puts the dji-thermal-ui command on your path: see First run.

items.title: From a clone
items.text:
A clone of the repository builds the pages with Node.js (24 or newer, with npm) and this documentation with Zensical:

uv sync
npm ci && npm run build
uv run --only-group docs zensical build --strict
uv run dji-thermal-ui

items.title: With the script
items.text:
On Linux, WSL or macOS, dji-thermal-ui.sh at the top of the clone does those steps and runs the app in the background:

./dji-thermal-ui.sh start

It builds the clone first if it was never built, then serves the app on http://127.0.0.1:8080. After pulling a newer version, ./dji-thermal-ui.sh build brings the environment, the pages and the documentation up to date, and ./dji-thermal-ui.sh restart runs it. Without uv, the script installs it into ~/.local/bin first (without changing the shell's startup files); without Node.js and npm, it stops and says where to get them. Its other commands are in The command.

items.title: Compare
items.text:
The compare page shows two datasets side by side, one over the other, or their difference, from any flight, the project's listed first. Open it with Compare with… in the viewer's header or on a dataset's card.

  • A pane shows a dataset's mosaic, or its visual mosaic.
  • Overlay (A over B) draws pane A's mosaic over pane B's in one pane, faded with an opacity slider and cut at a swipe line dragged across it: visual over thermal, or two thermal mosaics.
  • The difference of two mosaics, in one pane.

The header's Link the panes, Shared palette and Findings stay pressed in, with a check, while they are on.

Each pane draws its flights' findings, and a spot or an area drawn with the tools on a pane's map is measured there, opens its source frames, or is kept as a finding.

items.title: Datasets
items.text: A dataset is a flight's images converted to temperatures with dji-thermal-cli's settings, with its mosaics. They are on the flight page's Datasets tab, where the page opens once there is one.

items.title: Converting
items.text:
The tab lists the flight's datasets first, then the New dataset bar: the settings summed up and the Convert button. Change settings shows them all, each output named for what it is for, with dji-thermal-cli's name beside it. A problem a setting fixes opens this form with that setting already changed.

A dataset left unnamed is named after the settings that change its temperatures or mosaics ("Emissivity 0.9 · normalized", else "Default settings"), as the name field shows before converting.

You can keep several datasets side by side, cancel one while it converts, or download it.

items.title: The outputs
items.text:
• Temperatures as TIFFs, which WebODM can process.
  • The mosaics, opened in the viewer.
  • The visual mosaic: when a flight has visual images, a dataset builds their mosaic with the thermal ones ("And the visual mosaic", on by default), at the visual camera's own resolution. dji-thermal-cli places each visual image where its thermal frame is in the thermal mosaic, after measuring and correcting the small angle between the two cameras, so the two mosaics line up. Zoom camera images are left out. It is in the downloads beside the thermal mosaics.
  • R-JPEG (rjpeg) writes each frame again as an R-JPEG with the dataset's measurement parameters in DJI's header, so DJI's own tools measure it as this app does. Its picture, what photo viewers show, is coloured with the dataset's palette or kept as DJI's.

items.title: A dataset's card
items.text:
Each dataset on the tab has a card with its settings and progress. Its button is View mosaics once the mosaics are built (else Frames, or Cancel while it converts), and its menu (More) has:

  • Frames, the frames explorer, and Compare with…, the compare page.
  • Download all, the dataset's files as a zip, made as it downloads.
  • Files, its files listed on the card, each opening its frame.
  • Use settings, its settings put back in the New dataset form.
  • Build mosaics, when they were not built with it.
  • Process in WebODM (see WebODM).
  • Rename and Delete.

items.title: Exports
items.text:
Export… opens the Export dialog:

  • on the frame page, for the frame shown, as converted or with the parameters changed;
  • on the flight page's Files tab, for the frames the filter shows or all of them, measured with one of the flight's datasets or the frames' own values, with a palette and one range shared by all of them;
  • on the viewer, for the mosaic tab shown.

items.title: The formats
items.text:
A frame, the frames chosen or a whole flight export as:

  • Original: the files as they are.
  • TIFF: the temperatures.
  • PNG: coloured as the view, one pixel per sensor pixel.
  • R-JPEG: DJI's format, with the measurement parameters in its header.

A mosaic exports as its GeoTIFF, or a PNG of the view at full size.

Each format says what it is for. R-JPEG and Original are turned off, with the reason, for a normalized dataset or replaced values, which only TIFF carries.

items.title: Private
items.text: Each format can also be Private: without the location, the serial numbers and the free-text fields where a name or an email address could be. A private mosaic's GeoTIFF has no place.

items.title: Downloads
items.text: Several files come as a zip, made as it downloads. Export PNG, in the viewer, still saves the view as shown.

items.title: Findings
items.text: A finding is a spot or an area of a mosaic kept on its flight, with a name, notes, a severity and a status, the temperatures measured when it was kept, and the frames that saw it (all of them, or those you pick).

items.title: Keeping one
items.text:
• Draw a spot or an area on a mosaic and press Keep as finding on its card: the form opens with the frames beside it.
  • Or keep one from the source frames window, or from a saved spot or area measurement.

items.title: On the viewer
items.text: The viewer draws the findings on the map, outlined and tagged in their severity's colour. Click one, or its line in the side panel's Findings list (under Kept), to open it with its frames and change it. They can all be hidden with one switch, or one by one, and a link keeps which are shown and which is open.

items.title: On the compare page
items.text: On the compare page each pane draws its flights' findings, opened with a click or a link and changed there. A spot or an area drawn in a pane is kept on the flight of its mosaic (for a difference, the mosaic picked in the window).

items.title: Elsewhere
items.text: A project's page lists its flights' findings together. The reports list them with thumbnails of their kept frames, numbered on their maps. A saved video frame can be attached to a finding.

items.title: Flights
items.text: A flight holds the images of one flight of the drone. Its page has the flight's figures and its tabs: Files, Videos, Problems, WebODM plan and Datasets.

items.title: Making a flight
items.text:
New Flight on a project's page names the flight and takes its images, chosen one by one (Choose images) or as a folder (Choose a folder), with their thumbnails. The images can also be dropped on the project's page. Add images on the flight's page adds more later.

  • Thermal images: DJI R-JPEGs.
  • Visual images the drone takes with them (DJI's _V or _W, as on the Matrice 4T or the H20T/H30T). The Files tab calls them visual and shows what their metadata records (time, position, height, gimbal pitch and yaw, the rangefinder's distance), with no temperatures or measurement settings.
  • Videos: the drone's MP4s (see Videos).

Other files, such as TIFFs (a converted dataset's temperatures among them), cannot make a flight and are left out. A flight made in place from a folder by an earlier version still reads its images there.

items.title: The analysis
items.text: Once the images are in, dji-thermal-cli analyzes the flight: its files, cameras and the problems it finds. While it runs the page shows its progress; after it, a flight with no dataset yet says so above its tabs, with the way to convert it.

items.title: Problems
items.text:
The Problems tab lists each problem dji-thermal-cli finds, in the New dataset form's words, its temperatures in the unit chosen under User Preferences, and its files listed with their values (each opening the Files tab on it). The problem's code is the badge's tooltip.

A problem a setting fixes has a button that opens the Datasets tab with that setting changed in the New dataset form, converting nothing: normalizing the frames, one emissivity or humidity, the embedded or one fixed distance, or the oblique frames included when too few nadir frames are left.

items.title: Files
items.text:
The Files tab lists a flight's files, sorted by any column.

  • Filtering: conditions on any column (Height ≤ 21, Min > 32 °F, Kind is one of Thermal…), every one of which a file shown matches: numbers in the unit shown, text by its words. The Kind column's checkboxes and the Problems column (yes or no) filter too. All files, Thermal frames and With problems set the filter they stand for, to change from there.
  • Problems column: names each problem a file is in (Unusual max, Oblique…), with its sentence as the tooltip, and why a file isn't used.
  • Favourites: the filter is kept in the page's link, and can be saved under a name as a favourite, offered on every flight's Files tab. A favourite is deleted, never overwritten.
  • Hover for detail (checked by default, remembered by the browser): a pane at the right shows a file's picture, larger (a video's cover), and its columns as the pointer passes over its thumbnail or name. Clicking a row keeps it there until it is clicked again or closed (×, or Escape); unchecked, only a clicked row opens the pane.
  • Full size, in the pane, shows the picture at its own size over the page: fitting the window at first, zoomed with the wheel or shown 1:1, and moved by dragging. Escape or × closes it.

The tab's thermal pictures (thumbnails, pane and full size) are coloured with the palette chosen under User Preferences, over each frame's own range; with "As each flight's images" they are the camera's own pictures. Export… exports the frames the filter shows, or all of them (see Exports).

items.title: Videos
items.text:
The Videos tab lists a flight's videos with their covers, length, start time and drone. The one chosen plays beside a map of its track, with a marker on the frame shown, and a click on the track goes to that moment. Under it are the frame's time and number, height above take-off, gimbal pitch and yaw, heading, speed and position.

DJI's newer drones (the Matrice 4T among them) write no SRT: the track is read from the metadata DJI puts in the MP4, a point per frame, with nothing more installed, and the browser plays the video. A video's picture has the palette already applied, with a range that changes from frame to frame: it holds no temperatures.

items.title: Playback
items.text:
A frame or a second back or on, ⅛× to 2×, and a loop between an in and an out point at any speed.

Key Space play and pause Left Right a frame back or on (with Shift, a second) I O set the in and out points L turn the loop on and off - + change the speed S save the frame shown

items.title: Recoloured
items.text:
The frame shown can be turned back into the camera's levels (0 to 255) through DJI's Ironbow, then drawn in any palette, with a range (Auto takes the frame's 2nd to 98th percentile, and the range stays put from frame to frame), brightness, contrast, gamma, sharpening and an isotherm in levels. It starts as filmed (DJI ironred, 0 to 255). The pointer gives the level and pixel under it.

Levels are relative: the camera re-ranges each frame, so a level is not the same heat from one frame to the next. The Ironbow table is the Matrice 4T's.

items.title: Saved frames
items.text: Save frame (or S) keeps the frame shown, as shown (recoloured or as filmed), with its time, the drone's position, height and gimbal, and how it was coloured. They are listed under the video: a click on one goes back to that frame as it was shown. Each has a name, notes and a finding it can be attached to, and can be deleted. The flight report shows them, numbered V1, V2… on its map, and a finding's reports show those attached to it. A project's export carries them.

items.title: WebODM plan
items.text: The WebODM plan tab says how the flight would be processed in WebODM: its coverage, the task options recommended and those to consider, and how to prepare the images. See WebODM.

items.title: Deleting
items.text: Deleting a flight deletes only what the app made: a flight read in place from a folder leaves its images there.

items.title: Frames explorer
items.text: The frame page shows a dataset's frames one at a time, as converted, opened with Frames on its card or in the viewer's header.

items.title: The list
items.text:
The frames are listed beside the frame shown, in the order they were taken. Once the mosaics are built, a switch shows all of them, those In the mosaic (the frames the mosaic placed) or the Oblique ones (those it left out for their angle, whose angles show what a view straight down misses, including those a conversion with a pitch limit did not convert), with their counts. The switch is kept in the page's address.

They are listed as a list (name, time, and whether a frame is in the mosaic, oblique at its angle, left out as unusable or not converted) or as thumbnails, a switch the browser remembers.

The first is shown on opening; a click or Left Right shows another.

items.title: The frame
items.text: The frame has the viewer's palette, range, image sliders, Pointer info and measuring. Its Thermal/Visual/Both switch shows the frame's visual image in its place or beside it, with the same shapes and the cursor on it, and measures the thermal frame under them. A frame can be measured again with other parameters.

items.title: The map
items.text:
Its small map shows where the frames were taken. It can show the flight's visual photos too (orange squares), a switch the browser remembers.

Export… exports the frame shown, as converted or with the parameters changed (see Exports).

items.title: The maps under the mosaics
items.text:
The switch at the top right of a mosaic's map chooses what is under it. Every map starts with the one chosen under User Preferences › Map (ESRI Satellite unless another is chosen), and switching changes that map only.

  • ESRI Satellite (the default) and OpenStreetMap need nothing set up. Where Esri's imagery stops short of the zoom shown, its deepest level there is stretched instead of showing "Map data not yet available".
  • Mapbox Satellite needs a Mapbox account of your own and its access token, saved under System Settings. The switch lists it once a token is known.
  • None shows the mosaic alone, and loads nothing from the internet.

items.title: Getting the token
items.text:
1. Sign up at mapbox.com: no card is needed. The imagery comes through Mapbox's Static Tiles API, whose free allowance is 200,000 tiles a month; Mapbox charges past it only when a card is on the account.
  2. On the Access tokens page, copy the Default public token (it starts with pk.), or create a token with the public scopes only. A secret token (sk.) is refused: the browser sends the token to Mapbox with each tile, so anyone using the page could read it. Mapbox's URL restrictions do not accept 127.0.0.1, so leave the token unrestricted.
  3. Paste it under System Settings › Mapbox Satellite and press Check and save. Mapbox's Statistics page shows how many tiles have been used.

The app first asks Mapbox for one tile with the token, and saves it only if Mapbox serves it. Otherwise it says why (a wrong token, the account's limit, or Mapbox out of reach), and nothing is changed.

items.title: Where it is kept
items.text:
The token is kept as MAPBOX_API_TOKEN in a .env file: the one in the folder the app is started from or in the data folder, whichever it was read from (else the data folder's, made readable by you only). A new token replaces the old one in that file, the file's other lines kept; no earlier token is kept, and a token can be replaced but not removed there.

You can also write MAPBOX_API_TOKEN=pk.... in one of those files yourself. A MAPBOX_API_TOKEN in the environment the app is started from wins over the files: System Settings then shows it, and it is changed there. A token saved by an earlier version of the app (in its preferences) is moved to the data folder's .env when the app starts, unless a token is already known.

items.title: Measuring
items.text: Spots, lines, areas, boxes and circles are measured on mosaics, in the viewer and on the compare page, and on single frames, on the frame page.

items.title: Drawing a shape
items.text:
The drawing tools are on the map's top edge, beside the zoom buttons. A shape drawn is measured in a card on the map, closed with × or Escape. The card gives the temperature at a spot, or a shape's mean, min, max and standard deviation, its surroundings and the ΔT against them, the share inside the isotherm, its pixels, and a line's profile or an area's histogram.

On the card:

  • Save measurement keeps it, listed in the side panel under Kept.
  • Keep as finding, for a spot or an area of a mosaic: see Findings.
  • Source frames, for a spot or an area of a mosaic: see below.

On a frame page, the Thermal/Visual/Both switch shows the frame's visual image in its place or beside it, with the same shapes and the cursor on it, and measures the thermal frame under them.

items.title: Saved measurements
items.text: Saved measurements can be compared, measured again with other settings, and exported as CSV and GeoJSON. Each can have a comment, shown in the viewer's list, in the CSV and GeoJSON, and in the mosaic report.

items.title: Source frames
items.text:
The source frames window shows every frame that saw a spot or an area of a mosaic, the one the mosaic used first, each with its time and view angle and the spot marked or the area outlined in it, in the thermal frame or, with the Thermal/Visual switch, its visual image.

It opens from:

  • Source frames on a measurement's card;
  • a spot or an area drawn (or a click) on the Source frame or Visual tab;
  • a saved measurement's;
  • on the compare page, a spot or an area drawn with the tools on a pane's map.

A finding can be kept from it. Mosaics built before version 0.5.0 list only the frames they used: build them again to list every frame.

items.title: Mosaics
items.text: The viewer shows a dataset's mosaics, opened with View mosaics on its card or from the navigation pane.

items.title: The tabs
items.text:
Each tab's tooltip says what it shows.

  • Mosaic: each pixel is one frame's own temperature, as the frames were converted.
  • Harmonized: normalized, with one ambient and reflected temperature for every frame, and each frame's offset against its neighbours removed (the camera's drift between recalibrations), so the seams don't show as bands.
  • Source frame: which frame each pixel comes from (the one that saw it closest to straight down), with a line along each seam between the frames (in the mosaic report too).
  • View angle: how far from straight down each pixel was seen, in degrees.
  • Visual: the visual mosaic, when the dataset has one: the visual camera's images, each placed where its thermal frame is. Pointer info gives the Mosaic tab's temperatures, and a click opens the frames that saw the spot.
  • WebODM and Heights: an orthophoto and a surface model brought back from WebODM.

The viewer opens on Mosaic, or on Harmonized when the frames disagree (their offsets against their neighbours spanning more than 3 °C over the middle 90% of them), with a notice saying so. A link that names a tab opens that one.

Under the mosaic is a street map or satellite imagery, chosen with the switch at the top right of the map (see The maps under the mosaics).

items.title: The side panel
items.text:
The panel is grouped under:

  • View: the palette, the temperature range, Image (brightness and contrast, gamma, equalization and sharpening) and Isotherm. They are redrawn as their sliders are dragged. The colour scale is labelled with its range's ends.
  • Values: Pointer info (the values under the cursor), Parameters and This mosaic.
  • Kept: the saved measurements and the findings.
  • About.

On a first visit Image, Parameters, This mosaic and The mosaic start folded, and each section then stays as it was left.

items.title: Pointer info
items.text: Pointer info gives the values under the cursor. A click keeps them and outlines the frame there; Escape or a second click on that frame lets go of it.

items.title: From the viewer
items.text: The viewer's header has Frames (the frames explorer), Compare with… (the compare page), Export PNG (the mosaic as shown, with its saved measurements and colour scale, the basemap left out), Export… (the mosaic whole, at full resolution: see Exports) and Mosaic report (see Reports).

items.title: Projects
items.text: A project holds a site's flights together, with a name, a description and a location, and a map of where each flight was flown. The projects page lists them; a project's page lists its flights, with New Flight to add one.

items.title: Making and changing a project
items.text: New Project on the projects page asks for its name, description and location; the project's own page changes them later. The flights made before projects existed are in the Default Project, which you can rename, and one is made again whenever none is left. A flight is moved to another project with Move to another project in its row's menu on its project's page, which also has Rename, Analyze again and Delete.

items.title: The location
items.text: A project's location is found by searching an address or a place on OpenStreetMap, or by clicking the site on the map, and keeps the address. The search sends what is typed, or the point clicked, to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim: see What needs the internet.

items.title: Its findings
items.text: A project's page lists its flights' findings together.

items.title: Exporting and importing
items.text:
A project is exported (backed up) as a .tar with all its flights or those chosen: their images (a flight read from a folder has them copied in), datasets, mosaics, measurements, findings and saved video frames. The export is written straight to the browser's download, so it needs no room in the data folder.

Import on the projects page makes such an archive a new project, here or on another computer. A name already in use gets a free one ("Roof (2)"), which you can change. Flights that were read from a folder come back as uploaded ones. An import needs about the archive's size free in the data folder, as it is unpacked there while it is sent. An archive made on Linux can hold a file another system can't keep: a name with a colon or a question mark on Windows, or two names that differ only in case on Windows and macOS. The import stops and says which file.

items.title: Deleting
items.text: Deleting a project deletes its flights, after saying how many there are and how much space is freed. As with a flight, only what the app made is deleted: a flight read in place from a folder leaves its images there.

items.title: Reports
items.text: The two reports are pages laid out to print, or to save as PDF from the browser's print dialog, on A4 or Letter. They always print light, without the app's header and controls.

items.title: Flight report
items.text:
Opened with the flight page's Flight report button, it holds:

  • the flight's figures;
  • a map of where its frames were taken, with its findings and saved video frames numbered (V1, V2…), and the visual photos when they are put on it;
  • the coverage, and the problems found;
  • the frames' settings and temperatures summed up, and the datasets;
  • the findings, with thumbnails of their kept frames, and the video frames saved;
  • a table of every frame, when it is appended.

The title, author, date and notes are typed on the page and saved with the flight as typing pauses (the bar above says so: Saving…, then Saved). The last author typed fills in new reports.

items.title: Mosaic report
items.text:
Opened with Mosaic report in the viewer's header, it shows the mosaic as the viewer showed it when the button was pressed (that view is saved with the report), with:

  • the saved measurements and the flight's findings drawn and numbered, the colour scale, a scale bar and north;
  • each measurement, with a close-up on its mosaic or frame, its figures, profile and histogram, and a comment; one can be left out;
  • the findings on the mosaic, with their kept frames;
  • the dataset's settings, and how the mosaic was made (and when its heights came from a WebODM DSM).

A measurement's comment is also shown in the viewer's list and exported in the CSV and GeoJSON.

items.title: Printing
items.text: Print / Save as PDF opens the browser's print dialog, where the paper size is chosen and "Save as PDF" makes the file.

items.title: Preferences and settings
items.text: Both pages are in the navigation pane, with Storage. Each has a filter at the top, showing the sections whose title, labels, help or choices have the words typed ("dark" finds Theme).

items.title: User Preferences
items.text:
In the order the page has them:

  • Temperatures: the unit, °F, °C or K. Also in the header.
  • Palette: the palette the map pages start with: each flight's images' own, or one chosen. The viewer, the frames explorer, the compare page and the mosaic report open with it, and can still switch. A small made-up roof beside it shows the palette chosen.
  • Map: the map every map starts with: ESRI Satellite, OpenStreetMap, Mapbox Satellite once it has a token, or none. Each map can still switch, and a Mapbox that refuses its token goes back to ESRI Satellite. See The maps under the mosaics.
  • Theme: light or dark pages, or the computer's own. Also in the header.
  • Dates and times: the locale they are written in: the computer's, or one chosen.

A flight's capture times are shown in the time where it was flown, labelled with its time zone (for example UTC−5), found from the frames' two clocks. A flight analyzed by an earlier version of the app is analyzed again for it.

items.title: System Settings
items.text:
• Mapbox Satellite: the Mapbox token (see The maps under the mosaics).
  • WebODM: its address and login, with a short list of what connecting it brings (see WebODM).
  • A link to Storage.

items.title: Storage
items.text: The Storage page, in the navigation pane beside the other settings pages, shows where the data folder is, its size on disk as measured when the page opens (and again on asking) and the free space on its drive, with each project and its flights, the database and the rest. A flight read in place from a folder says how much its images take there, outside the data folder's total.

items.title: Moving the data folder
items.text:
The data folder can be moved from this page to another folder:

  1. Type the new folder's full path and check it. It may be a new folder, an empty one, or another data folder of this app. A folder holding other files is refused, as is one without room (on another drive, the whole data folder is copied there, then removed here). Nothing moves while a job runs or a project is being imported.
  2. Moving restarts the server. The database cannot change under a running server, so the server stops, moves the files as they are (same ids and links; a flight read in place is still read there) before it opens the database again, and starts again on the same port. The page reloads when it is back and says how the move went.

Another data folder there offers its projects, all chosen at first. Its database and files are set aside in replaced-<date>/ in it, nothing deleted; the projects chosen are then imported from them as an export would bring them (new ids, and a name already used gets a number), their files moved out of the folder set aside. A folder set aside stays in the data folder, counted under Other, and moves with it.

The new folder is remembered in a data-dir file in the app's config folder (see Where the data lives). --data-dir and DJI_THERMAL_UI_DATA_DIR still win, and a folder they set is not moved from the page. When the folder moved to is missing (a drive not connected), the app says so and stops rather than starting with an empty one.

items.title: WebODM
items.text: Processing with ODM is done in a WebODM of your own, through its API: DJI Thermal Analyzer sends a dataset's temperature TIFFs to it as a task, follows it, and can bring its orthophoto and surface model back. The flight page's WebODM plan tab says how the flight would be processed there.

items.title: Connecting it
items.text: The app logs in to WebODM as a WebODM account. Under System Settings › WebODM, give its address (http:// is fine, for a WebODM on this computer or your network), the account's user name and its password, and press Check and save. The app logs in to WebODM first and saves them only if WebODM takes them; it then lists the processing nodes the account can see. Otherwise it says why (a wrong login, WebODM out of reach, an address that isn't WebODM's) and nothing is changed.

items.title: Where the login is kept
items.text: The address, user name and password are kept as WEBODM_URL, WEBODM_USERNAME and WEBODM_PASSWORD in a .env file, as the Mapbox token is (the one they were read from, else the data folder's, made readable by you only), never in the database. The password is written encrypted (WEBODM_PASSWORD=enc:…, AES with a fresh random IV each time, so saving the same password twice gives two different values), with a key the app makes once and keeps in its database, not in .env: the file alone doesn't give the password away. A password typed into the file by hand is encrypted in place the next time the app starts; one set in the environment is left as it is. If the key is gone (the data folder's database replaced, or .env used with another data folder), System Settings › WebODM says the saved password can't be read: type it again. The page never shows the password, only that one is set, and shows the user name masked; leave either empty to keep the saved one. Remove takes all three out of the file, and the key out of the database. Set in the environment the app is started from, they win over the files: System Settings then shows them, and they are changed there. The app asks WebODM for a login token when it needs one and keeps it in memory only.

items.title: The account
items.text:
The account is set up by a WebODM admin, in WebODM's Administration (its /admin/ pages). System Settings › WebODM walks through it with the names those pages show, linking to them once WebODM's address is saved:

  1. Users › Add user: a user name and a password. Leave Active ticked, Staff status and Superuser status unticked: an ordinary account is enough.
  2. Its permissions. A new account is in WebODM's Default group, which holds these unless they were taken away from it (Groups › Default); else add them to the account under User permissions:
  3. app | Project | Can add Project (app.add_project): to create projects. The account owns those it creates, with every permission on them.
  4. app | Task | Can add Task, Can change Task and Can delete Task (app.add_task, app.change_task, app.delete_task): to create, upload to, follow, cancel and remove tasks.
  5. app | Preset | Can add Preset, Can change Preset and Can delete Preset (app.add_preset, app.change_preset, app.delete_preset): to keep task options as presets.
  6. nodeodm | Processing Node | Can view Processing Node (nodeodm.view_processingnode).
  7. Each processing node the account may use: Processing nodes › the node › Object permissions, type the user name in User identification, Manage user, choose Can view Processing Node and save (or the same for the Default group, under Groups). WebODM gives it to the Default group only for the node there when it first started: a node added later is not offered to the account until it, or its group, is given it.
  8. Only for a project the account didn't create: Projects › the project › Object permissions: Can view Project to see it, Can change Project to add tasks to it and Can delete Project to remove its tasks. A project shared with the account is never deleted through the API.
  9. Back in System Settings › WebODM, Check and save: the processing nodes the account sees are listed, and none means step 3 is missing.

items.title: Processing a dataset
items.text:
Once a dataset is converted with temperature TIFFs (temp_c:tiff), Process in WebODM in its card's menu makes a WebODM task from them:

  • The checks: a dataset still converting, one whose frames had their location removed, or one without at least two temperature TIFFs can't be sent. Settings that differ from the WebODM plan's (normalization, the pitch limit, the emissivity or humidity) are said, and can still be sent.
  • The project: a new WebODM project, named after the app's project unless you change it, or one of the account's, searched by name (one of the app's project's name is chosen when there is one). Nothing is remembered.
  • The options: the WebODM plan's, the recommended ones ticked and those to consider not, with the plan's reason for each; Add an option offers any other the processing nodes offer, with an input for its type. A WebODM preset (the account's or WebODM's own) can be applied: its options are ticked with its values, the others left as they are. The ticked options can be kept as a preset of the account's own (the same name changes it). The preset last applied is offered first next time.
  • The processing node (or WebODM's choice) and the task's name, "flight - dataset" unless changed.
  • Make a DSM: asks WebODM for a surface model as well (dsm, and fast-orthophoto left out, as it makes none), for the mosaics to be projected onto (below). The task takes longer.

Upload to WebODM sends the TIFFs in the background, beside conversions, so a long upload holds nothing up: the task is made waiting for its images, the TIFFs sent in batches, then the task committed and processed. An upload can be canceled; one canceled, refused or cut short by the app stopping removes the half-made task from WebODM (and the project, when it made it), at the next start if WebODM couldn't be reached.

The card lists the tasks made from the dataset, each with a link to it in WebODM and its progress: the upload's, then WebODM's while it is queued or processing (asked at most every 5 seconds while the page shows it). A task can be taken off the list; deleting the dataset does the same. Neither removes it from WebODM.

items.title: Bringing the results here
items.text:
Once WebODM has completed a task, Bring the orthophoto here on its line downloads its orthophoto in the background (with its progress, and a cancel). It is kept as temperatures, in the dataset's unit, and shown on the dataset's viewer as a WebODM tab beside its mosaics (even without mosaics of its own): coloured, read under the pointer, measured and saved as findings as they are, and offered on the compare page, beside the app's own mosaics or as their difference. ODM blends the frames, so it doesn't say which frames a spot came from. The orthophoto has to hold temperatures, which the WebODM plan's radiometric-calibration none keeps; one of colours is refused. A dataset shows one orthophoto: another task's replaces it. The card says which task it came from and can remove it; taking that task off the list removes it too. WebODM keeps its own copy either way.

A completed task that was asked for a DSM also has Bring the DSM here (one download per task at a time). The DSM is kept as WebODM wrote it, once dji-thermal-cli has read it, and the card says it is there:

  • Project the mosaics onto it: ticked when it arrives. The next time the mosaics are built, the frames are projected onto WebODM's surface instead of the heights dji-thermal-cli estimates from the frames themselves, so roofs and walls line up better at the seams. The mosaic's report says the heights came from the DSM.
  • The height cell: the size of the cells the surface is read on, in mosaic pixels (8 to 1024; 16 at first), with its size on the ground once the mosaics are built (16 px was about 24 cm in a test flight, and gave straight roof edges where the default 64 px stepped).
  • Build the mosaics again shows when the mosaics were built otherwise (without it, or on another cell).

A dataset keeps one DSM: another task's replaces it, keeping the tick and the cell. Remove, or taking its task off the list, removes it; the mosaics built on it are kept.

The DSM is also shown on the viewer, on a Heights tab: the height of the ground, roofs and trees in metres above the DSM's lowest ground (its 1st percentile, so a stray low pixel doesn't set it), with the palette (Viridis at first) and range as the View angle tab has them. On every tab, Pointer info gives the Ground height under the cursor (its tooltip, the height as WebODM gives it), and a spot measured on a temperature tab gets its ground height, an area its lowest, mean and highest.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
Six short tutorials, in order, from a first flight's images to its report. Each takes a few minutes, apart from the waits while the app works; the pictures were made on a real flight of a roof (its place left out).

  1. Make a project and a flight: the images uploaded and analyzed.
  2. Read the analysis: the flight's figures, its files and the problems found.
  3. Convert and open the mosaic: a dataset of temperatures, stitched into mosaics.
  4. Measure and keep a finding: a spot or an area measured, and kept with its frames.
  5. Print the reports: the flight's and the mosaic's, on paper or as PDF.
  6. Export: frames and mosaics as TIFF, PNG, R-JPEG or GeoTIFF.

Before you start, install the app and run it.

items.title: Read the analysis
items.text: Once dji-thermal-cli has read the images, the flight's page shows what it found: the flight's figures at the top, then its tabs.

items.title: 1. The figures
items.text: At the top: how many thermal frames there are (and visual images beside them), the camera, the range of the temperatures, when the flight was captured (in the time where it was flown), the median height, how many frames have a position, and the size on disk. A box under them says what comes next: making a dataset, in the next tutorial.

items.title: 2. The files
items.text:
The Files tab lists every file, with its kind, capture time, height, pitch and temperatures. Pass the pointer over a file's name: a pane at the right shows its picture and its columns. Click a row to keep it there, and Full size to see the picture at its own size.

Thermal frames and With problems filter the list; Add filter filters on any column, such as the height or the temperatures. See Files for all it can do.

items.title: 3. The problems
items.text:
The Problems tab lists what dji-thermal-cli found that could spoil the temperatures or the mosaics, such as frames much hotter than the rest or taken at an angle, with the files concerned. A problem a setting fixes has a button that puts that setting in the New dataset form.

Next: convert and open the mosaic.

items.title: Export
items.text: Export… saves frames or a mosaic in the format that suits what comes next.

items.title: 1. Frames
items.text:
On the flight's Files tab, Export… exports the frames the filter shows (all of them, unfiltered). Choose the format: PNG to look at, TIFF for the temperatures, R-JPEG for DJI's tools, or the files as the drone took them. The Private ones leave out the location, the serial numbers and the names. Then the dataset that measures them, and the palette and range of a PNG.

Press Export: several files come as a zip, made as it downloads.

items.title: 2. A mosaic
items.text:
In the viewer, Export… exports the mosaic tab shown, whole, at full resolution: as its GeoTIFF (private or not), or as a PNG.

See Exports for each format and when one is turned off.

items.title: Measure and keep a finding
items.text: A finding is a spot or an area kept on the flight with a name, notes, a severity and the frames that saw it: what a report is made of.

items.title: 1. Measure
items.text:
The drawing tools are on the map's top edge: a spot, a line, an area, a box and a circle. Choose the box and drag it across the place to measure. A card on the map gives its temperatures, the ΔT against its surroundings, and a histogram.

Save measurement keeps it as a measurement, listed in the panel under Kept. Here, keep it as a finding instead.

items.title: 2. Keep it as a finding
items.text:
Press Keep as finding on the card. The form opens over the frames that saw the area: give it a name, notes, a severity and a status, and choose the frames to keep with it.

Press Save. The finding is drawn on the map in its severity's colour, and opens with its frames when clicked.

See Findings and Measuring.

Next: print the reports.

items.title: Make a project and a flight
items.text: A project holds a site's flights; a flight holds the images of one flight of the drone. This tutorial makes both and uploads the images, which dji-thermal-cli then analyzes.
path: Make a project and a flight

items.title: 1. Make a project
items.text:
On the projects page (the app opens on it), press New Project at its top right.

Then give it a name and, if you like, a description. Its location is optional: search an address or click the site on the map, or leave it for later.

Press Create. The project's page opens, with no flights yet.
path: Make a project and a flight

items.title: 2. Make a flight
items.text:
Press New Flight, name the flight, then choose its images: Choose images for files picked one by one, or Choose a folder for a whole folder. Choose the thermal R-JPEGs, and the visual images (_V or _W) and videos the drone took with them if you have them: other files are left out. The dialog counts the images chosen.

Press Create. The images are uploaded, with their progress.
path: Make a project and a flight

items.title: 3. Wait for the analysis
items.text:
When the images are in, the flight's page opens and dji-thermal-cli reads them.

Next: read the analysis.
path: Make a project and a flight

items.title: Convert and open the mosaic
items.text: A dataset is the flight's images converted to temperatures, with mosaics stitched from them. A flight can have several, made with different settings.

items.title: 1. Make a dataset
items.text:
Press Make a dataset in the box above the tabs, or open the Datasets tab. The New dataset form starts from dji-thermal-cli's defaults, which suit most flights; Change settings shows them all. Leave the name empty to have the dataset named after its settings.

Press Convert. The dataset's card shows its progress: converting the frames, then building the mosaics. It can be cancelled.

items.title: 2. Open the mosaic
items.text:
When it is done, the card's button is View mosaics.

It opens the viewer, on the mosaic of temperatures. The tabs above the map show the same place in other ways (Harmonized evens out the frames' differences); the panel at the right sets the palette and the range, and Pointer info gives the temperature under the cursor.

See Mosaics for each tab and the panel's sections.

Next: measure and keep a finding.

items.title: Print the reports
items.text: Two reports are laid out to print, or to save as PDF from the browser's print dialog.

items.title: 1. The flight report
items.text:
Press Flight report on the flight's page. It holds the flight's figures, a map of where the frames were taken with the findings numbered, the problems, the datasets, and the findings with their frames. Type a title, the author and notes on the page: they are saved as you type.

Press Print / Save as PDF, and choose the paper size, or Save as PDF as the printer. The report always prints light, without the app's header and controls.

items.title: 2. The mosaic report
items.text:
In the viewer, set the mosaic as you want it shown (the tab, the palette, the range), then press Mosaic report. It shows the mosaic as the viewer did, with the measurements and findings numbered, the colour scale, a scale bar and north, then each measurement and finding in detail.

See Reports.

Next: export.

items.title: The command
items.text:
dji-thermal-ui [--data-dir DIR] [--port PORT] [--no-browser]

It serves the app on http://127.0.0.1:PORT and opens it in the browser. Ctrl+C stops it.

Option --data-dir DIR the folder for the database and the flights (see Where the data lives) --port PORT the port to serve on (default 8080) --no-browser do not open the browser --version print the version

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Variable DJI_THERMAL_UI_DATA_DIR the data folder, as --data-dir (which wins over it) DJI_THERMAL_UI_CONFIG_DIR the config folder, where a data folder moved from the Storage page is remembered MAPBOX_API_TOKEN the Mapbox token (see The maps under the mosaics) WEBODM_URL, WEBODM_USERNAME, WEBODM_PASSWORD WebODM's address and login (see WebODM)

The Mapbox token and WebODM's login are read from a .env file too, in the folder the app is started from or in the data folder; those set in the environment win over the files.

items.title: dji-thermal-ui.sh
items.text:
In a clone of the repository, on Linux, WSL or macOS, dji-thermal-ui.sh builds the app and runs it in the background:

Command ./dji-thermal-ui.sh build set up the environment, or bring it up to date: uv sync --locked, npm ci, npm run build and the documentation's build (Zensical). It does not pull: the code checked out is used as it is. Without uv, it installs uv into ~/.local/bin first (without changing the shell's startup files); without Node.js and npm, it stops and says where to get them. ./dji-thermal-ui.sh rebuild the same as build ./dji-thermal-ui.sh start start the app in the background, on http://127.0.0.1:8080, building it first if it was never built. Options after start go to the command: --port, --data-dir, --no-browser. ./dji-thermal-ui.sh stop stop it (as Ctrl+C would) ./dji-thermal-ui.sh restart stop, then start, with the options given ./dji-thermal-ui.sh status whether it runs, and at which address (exit status 3 when it does not) ./dji-thermal-ui.sh logs the end of its log; logs -f follows it

Its PID file and log are in .run/ in the clone (DJI_THERMAL_UI_RUN_DIR puts them elsewhere).

items.title: The data folder
items.text:
The database (SQLite), the secret key and each flight's files (datasets/<id>/) are kept in one data folder:

System Folder Linux ~/.local/share/dji-thermal-ui macOS ~/Library/Application Support/dji-thermal-ui Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\dji-thermal-ui

--data-dir or the DJI_THERMAL_UI_DATA_DIR environment variable uses another folder. Otherwise, a folder it was moved to from the Storage page is used. The Storage page shows which folder is used and what takes room in it, and moves it to another.

items.title: The config folder
items.text:
A data folder moved to from the Storage page is remembered in a data-dir file in the app's config folder:

System Folder Linux ~/.config/dji-thermal-ui macOS ~/Library/Application Support/dji-thermal-ui Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\dji-thermal-ui

DJI_THERMAL_UI_CONFIG_DIR uses another folder.

items.title: What deleting removes
items.text: A flight used in place from a folder (made by an earlier version) reads its images there and never changes them. Deleting a flight deletes only what the app made. Deleting a project deletes its flights the same way, after saying how many there are and how much space is freed.

items.title: Exports and imports
items.text:
A project's export is written straight to the browser's download, so it needs no room in the data folder. It holds manifest.json (the project's rows) and each flight's files under datasets/<id>/.

An import is unpacked as it is sent into imports/ in the data folder, then moved into place: it needs about the archive's size free there (no second copy of the archive is kept). An import a stopped server left half way is removed at the next start.
